claims.text: Adjusting the precursor addition rate modulates the instantaneous concentrations of metal-cation precursors.
Modulating instantaneous precursor concentrations can manipulate relative metal-reduction kinetics independently of intrinsic differences in reduction rate.
Precursor-addition-rate control synchronizes the reduction of metals having different reduction potentials.
Synchronized metal reduction drives simultaneous nucleation.
Simultaneous nucleation promotes uniform atomic mixing and thereby favors a single-phase solid solution.
Asynchronous reduction of precursors with disparate intrinsic kinetics can produce phase-segregated multimetallic nanoparticles.
Asynchronous reduction produces non-uniform crystal structures and uncontrolled particle morphology.
The initial material is a mixture of more than five noble-metal cation precursors with disparate intrinsic reduction kinetics.
The controlled intervention is to vary precursor addition rate while otherwise retaining the rapid heating and cooling synthesis regime.
The addition-rate mechanism applies to noble-metal HEA systems containing more than five elements under rapid thermal cycling.
Temporal synchronization of reduction events controls nucleation and growth so that a homogeneous single phase forms instead of separate phases.
Increasing precursor addition rate increases the instantaneous concentration of metal ions.
A sufficiently high instantaneous concentration causes even intrinsically slower-reducing metals to reduce rapidly.
Without addition-rate control, slower-reducing metals lag and undergo sequential, non-overlapping reduction.
Relative to uncontrolled precursor addition, the intervention will yield a uniform, single-phase solid-solution HEA nanoparticle structure.
Relative to the baseline, the intervention will reduce elemental segregation.
Relative to the baseline, the intervention will produce more controlled particle morphology.
Solvent, temperature, overall concentration, and scale may limit the validity of the proposed addition-rate mechanism.
EDX mapping, XRD, and HR-TEM can respectively assess elemental distribution, phase structure, and particle morphology or crystallinity in the test series.
Absence of a correlation between precursor addition rate and improved elemental uniformity or single-phase formation relative to the uncontrolled baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
